summary: The Lumber weight calculator works out thickness of a beam/plank from the length of a beam/plank, the width of a beam/plank, the weight of a beam/plank and the total volume. Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Nothing repaints underneath you: edit a field, press Calculate, and the new answer appears. That is how you find out which input the result is sensitive to.

sections.title: How does the Lumber weight calculator work?
sections.html:
The Lumber weight calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports thickness of a beam/plank in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type of wood); then you type in the length of a beam/plank, the width of a beam/plank, the weight of a beam/plank and the total volume.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Lumber weight calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Thickness of a beam/plank=volume of a beam ÷ plank ÷ (length of a beam ÷ plank × width of a beam ÷ plank)
Density=weight of a beam ÷ plank ÷ volume of a beam ÷ plank
Total weight=number of beams ÷ planks × weight of a beam ÷ plank
Volume of a beam/plank=total volume ÷ number of beams ÷ planks

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.html:

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Density, opening in pounds per cubic feet
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Lumber weight calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the length of a beam/plank, the width of a beam/plank and the weight of a beam/plank — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Lumber weight calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns thickness of a beam/plank, derived from the length of a beam/plank, the width of a beam/plank and the weight of a beam/plank. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Lumber weight calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length of a beam/plank, the width of a beam/plank, the weight of a beam/plank and the total volume, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter density in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Density opens in pounds per cubic feet and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Density = 0 lb/cu ft. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Lumber weight calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
